 Two people are on Agrihan and one is on Pagan as Typhoon In-fa closes in Friday, and the storm’s eye is wide enough to put Agrihan inside it even if the center passes to the north. Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Guam, provided those numbers Friday afternoon to The Guam Daily Post, saying he was relaying what he had been told. He said he knew of no evacuations.
 “As I understand, they should have sheltering capabilities either in a reinforced bunker or in a cave,” he said.
 The center of In-fa is forecast to pass just north of Agrihan between 6 and 8 p.m., Aydlett said, and the latest track has shifted, if anything, a mile or two north. With an eye this size, that margin means little.
 “It may not be passing directly over them as far as the center of the eye, because keep in mind this is about 45 to 50 miles across,” Aydlett said. “So even if the center of the eye is not over them, Agrihan may be well within the eye itself.”
 Inside the eye, winds could ease temporarily. The Weather Service’s 10 a.m. alert cautioned that the calm would not last because the eyewall would return from the other side. It warned residents of the three northern islands to remain in shelter until the storm passes.
 Typhoon warnings remain in effect for Alamagan, Pagan and Agrihan. At 1 p.m. Friday, the Weather Service placed the center about 95 miles east-southeast of Agrihan and 80 miles east of Pagan, moving west-northwest at 22 mph with sustained winds of 145 mph. Damaging winds of 39 mph or higher had already begun. Aydlett expects winds of 135 to 140 mph as the storm passes.
 The three islands will receive significant rainfall from the thick ring of thunderstorms surrounding the eye, he said.
 In-fa regained super typhoon strength overnight with winds of 150 mph before weakening to Category 4 around 1 p.m.
 “It really got its act together last night to have one last hurrah as a super typhoon,” Aydlett said.
 The drop was about 10 mph, he said, a relatively small change. Cooler water, increased wind shear to the northwest and a possible eyewall replacement cycle are expected to contribute to gradual weakening.
 The storm’s structure is unusual for the Marianas. Aydlett described it as an annular typhoon, with a large, open eye, a thick ring of thunderstorms and few rainbands extending outward. Typhoon-force winds extend up to 80 miles from the center.
 “We see annular typhoons, but usually more so in the western, northwestern Philippine Sea,” he said. “So to have this over here, it’s just spectacular to see it right on top of one of our islands.”
 Guam is about 355 miles from the storm’s center and will experience fair weather, Aydlett said, with northwest winds of 10 to 15 mph shifting to the southwest Friday night and the west Saturday and Sunday. Showers and thunderstorms are possible Sunday as winds weaken.
 Aydlett said, “we get off really easy with this one.”
 The main hazard for Guam is hazardous ocean conditions.
 “Even though the weather is great and it’s going to make the water seem inviting, we do have hazardous water conditions out there,” Aydlett said.
 A high surf advisory for Guam and Rota calls for waves of 10 to 14 feet along north- and east-facing reefs through 4 p.m. Saturday. A small craft advisory covers coastal waters around Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan.
 On Tinian and Saipan, a high surf warning for waves of 12 to 18 feet remains in effect until 4 p.m. Friday, followed by an advisory for waves of 8 to 12 feet through Saturday. The Weather Service said isolated coastal flooding of up to 1 foot is possible there.
 The swell will shift north, then northwest, the Weather Service said, increasing surf along west-facing reefs Friday night.
 Rip currents “can sweep even the best swimmers away from shore into deeper water.” Anyone caught in a rip current should relax and float, swim parallel to the shoreline if able, and call or wave for help.
 In-fa will not move away quickly. Aydlett said the storm will stall in the Philippine Sea as steering patterns shift and is not expected to accelerate until after Wednesday. That could bring northwest and west swells to the region into next week.
 “So it’s going to be in our backyard for quite a while,” he said.
 The Joint Typhoon Warning Center forecasts sustained winds of about 138 mph Saturday morning, 121 mph Sunday morning and 109 mph Wednesday morning. Aydlett said the storm should persist at least through midweek in an environment favorable for maintaining its strength. He said it is most likely to turn northeast into the open Pacific well east of Japan, avoiding the country.
